meta.titre: Dominant and Recessive Alleles: from genotype to offspring ratios

source.epreuve_titre: GCE O/L Human Biology past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: In a family in Yaounde, both parents have normal skin colour, yet their youngest child has albinism. Neighbours are surprised, but a geneticist is not. The explanation lies in the way alleles are inherited and in which of them is expressed. Questions on this topic appear every year at the GCE, from short definitions to crosses that ask you for a ratio or a probability, so a clear step-by-step method is worth learning.

items: A gene is a section of DNA on a chromosome that controls a characteristic.
Body cells carry chromosomes in pairs; sex cells (gametes) carry one chromosome of each pair.
At fertilisation a sperm and an egg fuse, so the child receives one set of chromosomes from each parent.

sections.titre: Dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous: reading and crossing genotypes
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Key ideas
Each gene exists in two or more forms called **alleles**. A person has two alleles of each gene, one inherited from each parent.

- A **dominant allele** shows its effect in the phenotype even when only one copy is present. It is written with a capital letter (for example **B**).
- A **recessive allele** shows its effect only when two copies are present. It is written with the same letter in lower case (**b**).

| Genotype | Name | Phenotype |
|---|---|---|
| BB | homozygous dominant | dominant trait |
| Bb | heterozygous (a carrier of b) | dominant trait |
| bb | homozygous recessive | recessive trait |

A **carrier** looks normal but can pass the recessive allele to children. Dominant does not mean "stronger" or "more common": it only describes which allele is expressed in a heterozygote.

### Method for a cross
1. Choose a letter and write the key (B = normal, b = albinism).
2. Write the genotypes of the parents.
3. Write the gametes. Each gamete carries **only one allele** of the gene, so Bb gives B and b.
4. Join every male gamete with every female gamete in a Punnett square.
5. Read the offspring genotypes, phenotypes and ratio.

| Cross | Offspring genotypes | Phenotypes |
|---|---|---|
| Bb $\times$ Bb | 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb | 3 dominant : 1 recessive |
| Bb $\times$ bb | 1 Bb : 1 bb | 1 dominant : 1 recessive |
| BB $\times$ bb | all Bb | all dominant |

The ratios are probabilities for each child, not a promise for a family of four.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the children are given and you must find the genotypes of the parents
variantes.contenu_markdown: A person showing the recessive trait must be **homozygous recessive** (bb), because one copy would be hidden. If two parents with the dominant trait have a child with the recessive trait, both parents must be **Bb**: each gave one b. A person with a dominant trait may be BB or Bb; a **test cross** with a bb partner decides. If any child shows the recessive trait the person is Bb; if many children all show the dominant trait the person is probably BB.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked for the chance that two or more children have a given trait
variantes.contenu_markdown: Each pregnancy is independent: earlier children do not change the chance for the next one. To find the chance of several events in a row, **multiply** the separate probabilities. If each child of two carriers has a probability of $\frac{1}{4}$ of being affected, the chance that the first two children are both affected is $\frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{16}$. Human examples: albinism and sickle-cell anaemia are both caused by recessive alleles.

sections.enonce_markdown: Sickle-cell anaemia is caused by a recessive allele. Let H be the allele for normal haemoglobin and h the allele for sickle-cell anaemia. Two healthy parents have a daughter with sickle-cell anaemia. (a) Give the genotypes of the two parents and explain your answer. (b) Draw a Punnett square for their next child. (c) State the probability that this child has sickle-cell anaemia, and the probability that it is a healthy carrier. *(8 marks)*

etapes.justification: The daughter has the recessive disease, so her genotype is known immediately. The parents show the dominant, healthy trait.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Daughter: hh. Parents: healthy, so each has at least one H.

etapes.justification: The daughter received one h from each parent. A parent who gave h but is healthy must also carry H.
Each parent makes two kinds of gamete in equal numbers.
Combine each gamete of one parent with each gamete of the other.
One square out of four is hh; two squares out of four are Hh.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Both parents are heterozygous (Hh), because each must carry h to give one to the daughter and each is healthy because of the dominant H. For each new child the probability of sickle-cell anaemia is 1 in 4 (25%), and the probability of a healthy carrier is 1 in 2 (50%). The probability of a child with two copies of H is also 1 in 4.

items.erreur_markdown: A dominant allele is always more common in the population than a recessive one.
items.pourquoi_faux: Dominance describes which allele is expressed in a heterozygote, not how many people carry it.
items.correction_markdown: Dominant means "expressed when only one copy is present"; it says nothing about how common the allele is.

items.erreur_markdown: The gametes of a Bb parent are written as Bb.
items.pourquoi_faux: A gamete has one allele of each gene, not two. Writing Bb shows two alleles in one sex cell.
items.correction_markdown: The gametes of a Bb parent are **B** and **b**, in equal numbers.

items.erreur_markdown: A 3 : 1 ratio means that a couple with four children will have exactly three normal and one affected child.
items.pourquoi_faux: The ratio is a probability applied to each child separately; chance can give any mixture in a small family.
items.correction_markdown: For each child the probability of the recessive trait is 1 in 4, whatever the earlier children are like.

items.erreur_markdown: A heterozygous person Bb shows a mixture of the dominant and recessive traits.
items.pourquoi_faux: In complete dominance the heterozygote shows only the dominant trait. The recessive allele is present but not expressed.
items.correction_markdown: Bb has the dominant phenotype and is a carrier of b.

items.enonce_markdown: For a certain human characteristic, D is the dominant allele and d is the recessive allele. For each of DD, Dd and dd, state whether the person is homozygous or heterozygous, and say which phenotype is shown. How many different kinds of gametes does a Dd person make?
items.solution_markdown:
- DD: **homozygous dominant**, dominant phenotype.
- Dd: **heterozygous**, dominant phenotype (a carrier of d).
- dd: **homozygous recessive**, recessive phenotype.

A Dd person makes **two** kinds of gamete, D and d.

items.enonce_markdown: Albinism is caused by a recessive allele a; the allele for normal pigment is A. A man with normal pigment and genotype Aa marries a woman with albinism. (a) Give her genotype. (b) Write the gametes of each parent. (c) Draw the Punnett square. (d) Give the ratio of normal to albino children and the probability that a child is a carrier.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) She shows the recessive trait, so she is **aa**.

(b) The man makes A and a. The woman makes only a.

(c)

| | a | a |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Aa | Aa |
| **a** | aa | aa |

(d) Two squares are Aa (normal) and two are aa (albino): the ratio is **1 normal : 1 albino**. The Aa children are carriers, so the probability that a child is a carrier is **$\frac{1}{2}$**.

items.enonce_markdown: A woman with normal pigment has a father with albinism. She marries a man with albinism. (a) Explain why her genotype must be Aa. (b) What is the probability that their first child has albinism? (c) What is the probability that their first two children both have albinism? (d) If the first child has albinism, does this change the probability for the second child? Explain.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Her father is aa, so he gave her an a. She has normal pigment, so her other allele must be A. Her genotype is **Aa**.

(b) Aa $\times$ aa gives 1 Aa : 1 aa, so the probability is **$\frac{1}{2}$**.

(c) $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} =$ **$\frac{1}{4}$**.

(d) **No**. Each child is a separate chance event, so the probability for the second child is still $\frac{1}{2}$.

items_markdown: A dominant allele (capital letter) is expressed when one copy is present; a recessive allele (lower case) is expressed only when two copies are present.
Homozygous means two identical alleles (BB or bb); heterozygous means two different alleles (Bb). A carrier is heterozygous and has the dominant phenotype.
Follow the method: key, parent genotypes, gametes (one allele each), Punnett square, ratio or probability.
Bb $\times$ Bb gives 3 dominant : 1 recessive; Bb $\times$ bb gives 1 : 1; the chance of a recessive child from two carriers is $\frac{1}{4}$.
A recessive child of two dominant parents means that both parents are heterozygous. Probabilities of independent events are multiplied.
